$\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)dy = \left(xy + \left({x}^{3} + 2\right)\sqrt{3\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)}\right)dx \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{xy}{1 - {x}^{2}} = \frac{\left({x}^{3} + 2\right)\sqrt{3\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)}}{1 - {x}^{2}}$

The above equation is a linear differential equation,

So, $\mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ - \int \frac{x}{1 - {x}^{2}}dx} = {e}^{\frac{1}{2}\ln \left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)} = \sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}}$

Now, the solution of the differential equation is given by,

$y\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} = \int \frac{\left({x}^{3} + 2\right)\sqrt{3\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)}}{1 - {x}^{2}} \times \sqrt{\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)}dx \implies y\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} = \sqrt{3} \int \left({x}^{3} + 2\right)dx \implies y\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} = \sqrt{3}\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4} + 2x\right) + c$

Now, using $y(0) = 0$ we get, $c = 0$

Now, finding $y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) y\sqrt{1 - {\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}} = \sqrt{3}\left(\frac{1}{{2}^{4} \cdot 4} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\right) \implies y = \left(\frac{1}{32} + 2\right) \implies y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{65}{32} = \frac{m}{n}$

Hence, $m + n = 97$

questions.question: Let the solution curve $x = x(y),0 < y < \frac{\pi }{2}$, of the differential equation ${\left({\log }_{e}\left(\cos y\right)\right)}^{2}\cos ydx - \left(1 + 3x{\log }_{e}\left(\cos y\right)\right)\sin ydy = 0$ satisfy $x\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2{\log }_{e}2}$. If $x\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) = \frac{1}{{\log }_{e}m - {\log }_{e}n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime, then $mn$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given,

${\left({\log }_{e}\left(\cos y\right)\right)}^{2}\cos ydx - \left(1 + 3x{\log }_{e}\left(\cos y\right)\right)\sin ydy = 0 \implies \frac{dx}{dy} + \left(\frac{ - 3\tan y}{\mathrm{lncos}y}\right)x = \frac{\sin y}{{\left(In\cos y\right)}^{2} \cdot \cos y}$

Which is a linear differential equation,

So, Integrating factor will be, $IF = {e}^{3 \int \frac{ - \tan y}{\mathrm{lncos}y}dy} = {\left(\mathrm{lncos}y\right)}^{3}$

So, solution of differential equation is given by,

$x{\left(\mathrm{lncos}y\right)}^{3} = \int \frac{\sin y}{\cos y}\left(\mathrm{lncos}y\right)dy \implies x{\left(\mathrm{lncos}y\right)}^{3} = \frac{ - {\left(\mathrm{lncos}y\right)}^{2}}{2} + c$

Now using the given value of $x\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2\ln 2}$

We get, $c = 0$

Hence, $x = \frac{ - 1}{2\ln \cos y}$

Now finding, $x\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) = - \frac{1}{2\ln \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} = \frac{1}{\ln 4 - \ln 3}$

Now on comparing with $\frac{1}{{\log }_{e}m - {\log }_{e}n}$ we get, $m = 4,n = 3$

Hence, $mn = 12$

questions.question: If for the solution curve $y=f(x)$ of the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}+(\tan x) y=\frac{2+\sec x}{(1+2 \sec x)^2}$, $x \in\left(\frac{-\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right), f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{10}$, then $f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
$\begin{aligned} & \text { If } \mathrm{e}^{\int \tan \mathrm{xdx}}=\mathrm{e}^{\ln (\sec \mathrm{x})}=\sec \mathrm{x} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{y} \cdot \sec \mathrm{x}=\int\left\{\frac{2+\sec \mathrm{x}}{(1+2 \sec \mathrm{x})^2}\right\} \sec \mathrm{xdx} \\ & =\int \frac{2 \cos \mathrm{x}+1}{(\cos \mathrm{x}+2)^2} \mathrm{dx} \text { Let } \cos \mathrm{x}=\frac{1-\mathrm{t}^2}{1+\mathrm{t}^2} \\ & =\int \frac{2\left(\frac{1-\mathrm{t}^2}{1+\mathrm{t}^2}\right)+1}{\left(\frac{1-\mathrm{t}^2}{1+\mathrm{t}^2}+2\right)^2} 2 \mathrm{dt}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & =\int \frac{2-2 t^2+1+t^2}{\left(1-t^2+2+2 t^2\right)^2} \times 2 \mathrm{dt} \\ & =2 \int \frac{3-t^2}{\left(t^2+3\right)^2} \mathrm{dt} \end{aligned}$

Let $\mathrm{t}+\frac{3}{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{u} \begin{aligned} & \left(1-\frac{3}{\mathrm{t}^2}\right) \mathrm{dt}=\mathrm{du} \\ & =-2 \int \frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{u}^2} \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & y \cdot(\sec x)=\frac{2}{u}+c \\ & y \cdot \sec x=\frac{2}{t+\frac{3}{t}}+c...(I) \end{aligned} \text { At } \mathrm{x}=\frac{\pi}{3}, \mathrm{t}=\tan \frac{\mathrm{x}}{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} 2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{10}=\frac{2}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+3 \sqrt{3}}+\mathrm{c} \begin{aligned} & \text { 2. } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{10}=\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{10}+\mathrm{c} \Rightarrow \mathrm{C}=0 \\ & \text { At } \mathrm{x}=\frac{\pi}{4}, \mathrm{t}=\tan \frac{\mathrm{x}}{2}=\sqrt{2}-1 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{y} \cdot \sqrt{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}-1+\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}-1}} \\ & \mathrm{y} \cdot \sqrt{2}=\frac{2(\sqrt{2}-1)}{6-2 \sqrt{2}} \\ & \mathrm{y}=\frac{\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}-1)}{2(3-\sqrt{2})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \times \frac{2 \sqrt{2}-1}{7} \\ & =\frac{4-\sqrt{2}}{14}\end{aligned}$

questions.question: If the solution curve of the differential equation $\left(\left({\tan }^{ - 1}y\right) - x\right)dy = \left(1 + {y}^{2}\right)dx$ passes through the point $\left(1,0\right)$ then the abscissa of the point on the curve whose ordinate is $\tan \left(1\right)$ is
questions.explanation:
$\left({\tan }^{ - 1}y - x\right)dy = \left(1 + {y}^{2}\right)dx \implies \frac{dx}{dy} + \left(\frac{1}{1 + {y}^{2}}\right)x = \frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}{1 + {y}^{2}}$

I.F. $= {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{1 + {y}^{2}}dy} = {e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}$

General solution will be

$x\left({e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}\right) = \int {e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y} \times \frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}{1 + {y}^{2}}dy \implies x\left({e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}\right) = {\tan }^{ - 1}y\left({e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}\right) - {e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y} + C$

Since the curve passes through $\left(1,0\right) \implies C = 2$

So, the curve reduces to $x\left({e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}\right) = {\tan }^{ - 1}y\left({e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y}\right) - {e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}y} + 2$

when $y = \tan 1,x\left(e\right) = 1\left(e\right) - e + 2 \implies x = \frac{2}{e}$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x}\left(1 + {x}^{2}\left(1 + {\log }_{e}x\right)\right)$, $x > 0,y(1) = 3$. Then $\frac{{y}^{2}(x)}{9}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation can be rewritten as,

$\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y}{x} = {y}^{3}\left(1 + {\log }_{e}x\right) \frac{1}{{y}^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}} - \frac{1}{{\mathrm{xy}}^{2}} = 1 + {\log }_{e}x$

Let $\left( - \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\right) = t \implies \frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}} = \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{dx}} ∴\frac{\mathrm{dt}}{2\mathrm{dx}} + \frac{t}{x} = \left(1 + {\log }_{e}x\right) \implies \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{dx}} + \frac{2t}{x} = 2\left(1 + {\log }_{e}x\right)..........(1)$

We know the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$ is given by,

${\mathrm{ye}}^{ \int \mathrm{Pdx}} = \int {\mathrm{Qe}}^{ \int \mathrm{Pdx}} + C(\mathrm{Where}I.F. = {e}^{ \int \mathrm{Pdx}})$

Therefore, on solving equation(1) we get,

I.F.$= {e}^{ \int \frac{2}{x}dx} = {x}^{2} \frac{ - {x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} = \frac{2}{3}\left(\left(1 + {\log }_{e}x\right){x}^{3} - \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right) + C......(2)$

Given,$y(1) = 3 \implies \frac{1}{9} = - 2\left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{9}\right) + C ∴C = \frac{5}{9}$

Now putting value of C in equation(2) we get,

$\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} = \frac{{x}^{2}}{5 - 2{x}^{3}\left(2 + {\log }_{e}{x}^{3}\right)}$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation, $\frac{dy}{dx} + y\tan x = 2x + {x}^{2}\tan x,x \in \left( - \frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\right),$ such that $y\left(0\right) = 1.$ Then
questions.explanation:
Given $\frac{dy}{dx} + y\tan x = 2x + {x}^{2}\tan x$

This is a linear differential equation of the type $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P = \tan x & Q = 2x + {x}^{2}\tan x$

Now, the integrating factor $I.F. = {e}^{ \int Pdx} = {e}^{ \int \tan xdx} = {e}^{\mathrm{lnsec}x} = \sec x$

And, the general solution is $y\left(I.F.\right) = \int Q\left(I.F.\right)dx + c y⋅\sec x = \int \left(2x + {x}^{2}\tan x\right)\sec xdx + c \implies ysecx = \int 2xsecxdx + \int {x}^{2}\left(\sec x⋅\tan x\right)dx + c$

Using integration by parts in the second integral, we get

$\implies ysecx = \int 2x\sec xdx + {x}^{2} \int \left(\sec x⋅\tan x\right)dx - \int \left(\frac{d}{dx}\left({x}^{2}\right) \int \left(\sec x⋅\tan x\right)\right)dx + c \implies ysecx = \int 2x\sec xdx + {x}^{2} \int secxdx - \int 2xsecxdx + c \implies ysecx = {x}^{2}secx + c \implies y = {x}^{2} + c \cdot \cos x$

Now, $y\left(0\right) = 1 \implies 0 + c = 1 \implies c = 1$

So, $y = {x}^{2} + cosx$

Hence, $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $y\left( - \frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Differentiating $y(x)$ with respect to $x \implies {y}^{'}\left(x\right) = 2x - sinx$

Hence, ${y}^{'}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{\pi }{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and ${y}^{'}\left( - \frac{\pi }{4}\right) = - \frac{\pi }{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \implies {y}^{'}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) - {y}^{'}\left( - \frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \pi - \sqrt{2}.$

questions.question: If the solution curve of the differential equation $\left(2x - 10{y}^{3}\right)dy + ydx = 0$, passes through the points $(0,1)$ and $(2,\beta )$, then $\beta$ is a root of the equation?
questions.explanation:
Given that: $\left(2x−10{y}^{3}\right)dy + ydx = 0 \implies \frac{dx}{dy} = 10{y}^{2} - \frac{2x}{y} \implies \frac{dx}{dy} + \frac{2x}{y} = 10{y}^{2} \implies \text{ I.F. } = {e}^{2 \int \frac{1}{y}dx} = {y}^{2} \implies x⋅{y}^{2} = \int 10{y}^{4}dy + C \implies x⋅{y}^{2} = 2{y}^{5} + c \mathrm{Put}x = 0 & y = 1 \implies \; \implies x⋅{y}^{2} = 2{y}^{5}−2$

Passing Through $(2,\beta ) \implies 2⋅{\beta }^{2} = 2{\beta }^{5}−2 \implies {\beta }^{5}−{\beta }^{2}−1 = 0$

root of the equations

${y}^{5} - {y}^{2} - 1 = 0$

questions.question: Let $x=x(y)$ be the solution of the differential equation $y^2 \mathrm{~d} x+\left(x-\frac{1}{y}\right) \mathrm{d} y=0$. If $x(1)=1$, then $x\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is :
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & y^2 d x+\left(x-\frac{1}{y}\right) d y=0 \\ & y^2 d x=\left(\frac{1}{y}-x\right) d y \\ & \Rightarrow y^2 \frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{1}{y}-x \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{d x}{d y}+\frac{x}{y^2}=\frac{1}{y^3} \\ & \text { I.F. }=e^{\int \frac{1}{y^2} d y}=e^{\frac{-1}{y}} \end{aligned} \therefore$ Solution is $x e^{\frac{-1}{y}}=\int e^{-\frac{1}{y}} \times \frac{1}{y^3} d y+C$ Let $\frac{-1}{y}=t \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{y^2} d y=d t \\ & \Rightarrow x e^{-\frac{1}{y}}=-\int e^t t d t+C \\ & \Rightarrow x e^{-\frac{1}{y}}=-e^t(t-1)+C \\ & \Rightarrow x e^{-\frac{1}{y}}=-e^{\frac{-1}{y}}\left(\frac{-1}{y}-1\right)+C \end{aligned} x(1)=1 \Rightarrow e^{-1}=-e^{-1}(-2)+C \Rightarrow C=-e^{-1} \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{y}+1-e^{-1+\frac{1}{y}} x\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=3-e$ .

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(t\right)$ be a solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dt} + \alpha y = \gamma {e}^{ - \beta t}$ Where, $\alpha > 0,\beta > 0$ and $\gamma > 0$. Then ${Lim}_{t \to \infty }y\left(t\right)$
questions.explanation:
Given,

$\frac{dy}{dt} + \alpha y = \gamma \cdot {e}^{ - \beta t}$

Which is a linear differential equation,

So, integrating factor will be $I.F = {e}^{ \int \alpha dt} = {e}^{\alpha t}$

So, the solution of differential equation is given by

$y \times {e}^{\alpha t} = \gamma \int {e}^{ - \beta t} \times {e}^{\alpha t} \implies y \times {e}^{\alpha t} = \gamma \int {e}^{\left(\alpha - \beta \right)t} \implies y \times {e}^{\alpha t} = \gamma \frac{{e}^{\left(\alpha - \beta \right)t}}{\left(\alpha - \beta \right)} + c \implies y = \gamma \frac{{e}^{ - \beta t}}{\left(\alpha - \beta \right)} + c{e}^{ - \alpha t}$

Now finding $\underset{t \to \infty }{\lim }y$ we get,

$\underset{t \to \infty }{\lim }y = \underset{t \to \infty }{\lim }\left(\gamma \frac{{e}^{ - \beta t}}{\left(\alpha - \beta \right)} + c{e}^{ - \alpha t}\right) \implies \underset{t \to \infty }{\lim }y = \gamma \times 0 + c \times 0 = 0\left(\text{as }{e}^{ - \infty } \to 0\right)$

;

questions.question: If a curve $y=y(x)$ passes through the point $\left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and satisfies the differential equation $\left(7 x^4 \cot y-e^x \operatorname{cosec} y\right) \frac{d x}{d y}=x^5, x \geq 1$, then at $x=2$, the value of cosy is:
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{7 \cot y}{x}-\frac{e^x \operatorname{cosec} y}{x^5} \\ & \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{7 \cot y}{\sin y \cdot x}-\frac{e^x}{\sin y x^5} \\ & \sin y \frac{d y}{d x}-\cos y \cdot \frac{7}{x}=\frac{-e^x}{x^5} \\ & \text { let }-\cos y=t \\ & \sin y \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d t}{d x}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \frac{d t}{d x}+\frac{7 t}{x}=\frac{-e^x}{x^5} \\ & \text { I.F. }=x^7 \\ & \text { t. } x^7=-\int x^2 e^x d x \\ & \operatorname{cosy} x^7=x^2 e^x-2 \int x e^x d x \\ & \operatorname{cosy} x^7=x^2 e^x-2 x e^x+2 e^x+c \\ & x=1, y=\frac{\pi}{2}, c=-e \\ & \operatorname{cosy}=\frac{2 e^2-e}{128} \\ & \text { option }(3)\end{aligned}$ `

questions.question: If $x = x\left(y\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $y\frac{dx}{dy} = 2x + {y}^{3}\left(y + 1\right){e}^{y},x\left(1\right) = 0$; then $x\left(e\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given

$\frac{dx}{dy} - \frac{2x}{y} = {y}^{2}\left(y + 1\right){e}^{y}$

Finding integrating factor $I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{−2}{y}dx} = {e}^{−2\ln y} = \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \implies \frac{x}{{y}^{2}} = \int \left(y + 1\right){e}^{y}dy \implies \frac{x}{{y}^{2}} = y \cdot {e}^{y} + C 0 = e + C \implies C = - e \implies \frac{x}{{y}^{2}} = y{e}^{y} - e$

Putting $y = e$ in the equation we get

$\implies \frac{x}{{e}^{2}} = e.{e}^{e} - e \implies x = {e}^{3}\left({e}^{e} - 1\right)$

!

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation, $x\frac{dy}{dx} + y = x{\log }_{e}x,\left(x > 1\right)$. If $2y\left(2\right) = {\log }_{e}4 - 1$, then $y\left(e\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation can be written as

$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{y}{x} = {\log }_{e}x$, which is a linear differential equation.

Now, integrating factor $I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{x}dx} = {e}^{lnx} = x$

Hence, the solution of the given differential equation is

$y \cdot x = \int x \cdot {\log }_{e}xdx \implies y \cdot x = {\log }_{e}x \int xdx - \int \left(\frac{1}{x} \int xdx\right)dx$ (using integration by parts)

$\implies y \cdot x = {\log }_{e}x\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) - \int \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}dx \implies y \cdot x = {\log }_{e}x\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) - \int \frac{x}{2}dx \implies xy\left(x\right) = \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{\log }_{e}x - \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} + C...\left(1\right)$

Putting $x = 2$ we get,

$\implies 2y\left(2\right) = 2{\log }_{e}2 - 1 + C \implies 2y\left(2\right) = {\log }_{e}4 - 1 + C$

Given, $2y\left(2\right) = {\log }_{e}4 - 1$

Then we get, $C = 0$

Now, from the equation $\left(1\right)$ we get,

$y\left(x\right) = \frac{x}{2}{\log }_{e}x - \frac{x}{4}$

Putting $x = e$ in above equation, we get,

$y\left(e\right) = \frac{e}{2}{\log }_{e}e - \frac{e}{4} = \frac{e}{2} - \frac{e}{4} = \frac{e}{4}$

!

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x{\left(x + y\right)}^{3}−x\left(x + y\right)−1,y\left(0\right) = 1$. Then, ${\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + y\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right)}^{2}$ equals:
questions.explanation:
Given: $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x{\left(x + y\right)}^{3}−x\left(x + y\right)−1$

Let, $x + y = t \implies 1 + \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx} - 1 \implies \frac{dt}{dx}−1 = 2x{t}^{3}−xt−1 \implies \frac{dt}{dx} = 2x{t}^{3}−xt \implies \frac{dt}{dx} + xt = 2x{t}^{3} \implies \frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\frac{dt}{dx} + \frac{x}{{t}^{2}} = 2x...\left(i\right)$

Putting, $\frac{1}{{t}^{2}} = u \implies \frac{ - 2}{{t}^{3}}\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{du}{dx} \implies \frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{ - 1}{2}\frac{du}{dx}$

Putting this value in equation $\left(i\right) \implies \frac{ - 1}{2}\frac{du}{dx} + xu = 2x \implies \frac{du}{dx} - 2xu = - 4x$

Integrating factor, $IF = {e}^{ \int - 2xdx} \implies IF = {e}^{ - {x}^{2}}$

So, solution of the given differential equation is,

$u \times {e}^{ - {x}^{2}} = \int {e}^{ - {x}^{2}}\left( - 4x\right)dx \implies \frac{{e}^{ - {x}^{2}}}{{t}^{2}} = \int {e}^{ - {x}^{2}}\left( - 4x\right)dx$

Putting, $- {x}^{2} = z \implies - 2xdx = dz \implies \frac{{e}^{ - {x}^{2}}}{{\left(x + y\right)}^{2}} = \int 2{e}^{z}dz \implies \frac{{e}^{ - {x}^{2}}}{{\left(x + y\right)}^{2}} = 2{e}^{z} + C \implies \frac{{e}^{ - {x}^{2}}}{{\left(x + y\right)}^{2}} = 2{e}^{ - {x}^{2}} + C \implies \frac{1}{{\left(x + y\right)}^{2}} = 2 + C{e}^{{x}^{2}}$

It is given that, at $x = 0$, $y = 1$.

$\implies 1 = 2 + C \implies C = - 1 \implies {\left(x + y\right)}^{2} = \frac{1}{2−{e}^{{x}^{2}}}$

Putting, $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \implies {\left(y + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}^{2} = \frac{1}{2−{e}^{\frac{1}{2}}} \implies {\left(y\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}^{2} = \left(\frac{1}{2−\sqrt{e}}\right)$

`

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x{\log }_{e}x\frac{dy}{dx} + y = {x}^{2}{\log }_{e}x,(x > 1)$. If $y(2) = 2$, then $y(e)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given,

$x\ln x\frac{dy}{dx} + y = {x}^{2}\ln x \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{y}{x\ln x} = x$

This is a linear differential equation.

Now, finding integrating factor we get

$I.F = {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{\mathrm{xlnx}}\mathrm{dx}} = {e}^{\ln \left(\mathrm{lnx}\right)} = \mathrm{lnx}$

Now, solution of the differential equation is given by

$y \times I.F = \int \left(x \times I.F\right)dx \implies y \times \ln x = \int \mathrm{xlnx}dx \implies y \times \ln x = \ln x \cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} - \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} + c$

Now given $y\left(2\right) = 2$,

$2 \times \ln 2 = \ln 2 \cdot \frac{{2}^{2}}{2} - \frac{{2}^{2}}{4} + c \implies c = 1$

So, equation will be $y \times \ln x = \ln x \cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} - \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} + 1$

Now finding $y\left(e\right)$ we get,

$y \times \ln e = \ln e \cdot \frac{{e}^{2}}{2} - \frac{{e}^{2}}{4} + 1 \implies y \times 1 = 1 \cdot \frac{{e}^{2}}{2} - \frac{{e}^{2}}{4} + 1 \implies y = \frac{4 + {e}^{2}}{4}$

;

questions.question: Suppose $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution curve to the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} - y = 2 - {e}^{ - x}$ such that $\underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }y\left(x\right)$ is finite. If $a$ and $b$ are respectively the $x -$ and $y -$intercept of the tangent to the curve at $x = 0$, then the value of $a - 4b$ is equal to _______.
questions.explanation:
Given,

$\frac{dy}{dx} - y = 2 - {e}^{ - x}$

Linear differential equation,

So, $I.F. = {e}^{ - \int \mathrm{dx}} = {e}^{ - x}$

Now solution of differential equation is given by

$y \times IF = \int \left(2 - {e}^{ - x}\right) \times IFdx \implies y{e}^{ - x} = \int \left(2 - {e}^{ - x}\right){e}^{ - x}dx \implies y{e}^{ - x} = \int \left(2{e}^{ - x} - {e}^{ - 2x}\right)dx \implies y{e}^{ - x} = - 2{e}^{ - x} + \frac{{e}^{ - 2x}}{2} + C \implies y = - 2 + \frac{{e}^{ - x}}{2} + C{e}^{x}$

Given $\underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }y$ is finite

So, $\underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }\left( - 2 + \frac{{e}^{ - x}}{2} + C \cdot {e}^{x}\right) \to$finite

This is possible only when $C = 0$

Hence$y = y\left(x\right) = - 2 + \frac{{e}^{ - x}}{2}$

Now finding the slope $\frac{dy}{dx} = - \frac{1}{2}{e}^{ - x} {\frac{dy}{dx}}_{x = 0} = - \frac{1}{2} = m,y\left(0\right) = - 2 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{ - 3}{2}$

Now equation of tangent will be,

$y + \frac{3}{2} = - \frac{1}{2}\left(x - 0\right) \implies x + 2y = - 3$

x-intercept $a = - 3,$ y-intercept $b = \frac{ - 3}{2}$

So, $a - 4b = - 3 + 6 = 3$

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}+2 y \sec ^2 x=2 \sec ^2 x+3 \tan x \cdot \sec ^2 x$ such that $\mathrm{y}(0)=\frac{5}{4}$. Then $12\left(\mathrm{y}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-\mathrm{e}^{-2}\right)$ is equal to _______.
questions.explanation:
$\begin{aligned} \text { I.F. } & =\mathrm{e}^{\int 2 \sec ^2 x d x} \\ & =\mathrm{e}^{2 \tan x}\end{aligned}$

Solution of diff. eq.

$\begin{gathered}y \cdot e^{2 \tan x}=\int e^{2 \tan x}\left(2 \sec ^2 x+3 \tan x \cdot \sec ^2 x\right) d x \\ y \cdot e^{2 \tan x}=\int e^{2 \tan x} \cdot\left(2 \sec ^2 x\right) d x+\int e^{2 \tan x} \cdot\left(3 \tan x \cdot \sec ^2 x\right) d x\end{gathered}$

y. $\mathrm{e}^{2 \tan x}=\mathrm{e}^{2 \tan x} \cdot 2 \tan x-\int \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan x} \cdot 2 \sec ^2 x \times 2 \tan x d x+\int \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan x} \cdot 3 \tan x \cdot \sec ^2 x d x \begin{aligned} & y \cdot e^{2 \tan x}=2 \tan x \cdot e^{2 \tan x}-\int \mathrm{e}^{2 \tan x} \cdot \tan x \sec ^2 x d x \\ & y . e^{2 \tan x}=2 \tan x \cdot e^{2 \tan x}-\frac{\tan x \cdot e^{2 \tan x}}{2}+\frac{e^{2 \tan x}}{4}+C\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & y=2 \tan x-\frac{\tan x}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\mathrm{Ce}^{-2 \tan x} \\ & x=0, y=\frac{5}{4} \\ & c=1\end{aligned} \mathrm{y}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{7}{4}+\mathrm{e}^{-2}$

Then $12\left(y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-\mathrm{e}^{-2}\right)=12\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)=21$

questions.question: Let the solution curve $y = y(x)$ of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{3{x}^{5}{\tan }^{ - 1}\left({x}^{3}\right)}{{\left(1 + {x}^{6}\right)}^{\frac{3}{2}}}y = 2x \exp \frac{{x}^{3} - {\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{(1 + x{)}^{6}}}$ pass through the origin. Then $y(1)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation is$\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(\frac{ - 3{x}^{5}{\tan }^{ - 1}\left({x}^{3}\right)}{{\left(1 + {x}^{6}\right)}^{3 / 2}}\right)y = 2x{e}^{\left(\frac{{x}^{3} - {\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{6}}}\right)}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$.

Hence,

$I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{ - 3{x}^{5}{\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3}}{{\left(1 + {x}^{6}\right)}^{3 / 2}}dx}$

Put ${\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3} = u \implies \left(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{1 + {x}^{6}}\right)dx = du I.F. = {e}^{ - \int \frac{u\tan u}{\sqrt{1 + {\tan }^{2}u}}du} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - \int \frac{u\tan u}{\sec u}du} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - \int u\sin udu} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - \left( - u\cos u + \int \cos udu\right)} \implies I.F. = {e}^{u\cos u - \sin u} \implies I.F. = {e}^{\left({\tan }^{ - 1}\left({x}^{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right) - \left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)\right)} \implies I.F. = {e}^{\left(\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3} - {x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)}$

Solution of differential equation is

$y \cdot {e}^{\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3} - {x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}} = \int 2x{e}^{\left(\frac{{x}^{3} - {\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)} \cdot {e}^{\left(\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left({x}^{3}\right) - {x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)}dx \implies y \cdot {e}^{\left(\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3} - {x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)} = \int 2xdx \implies y \cdot {e}^{\left(\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3} - {x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)} = {x}^{2} + C$

Also, it passes through the origin then $C = 0$, hence

$y{e}^{\left(\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}{x}^{3} - {x}^{3}}{\sqrt{1 + {x}^{6}}}\right)} = {x}^{2}$

Now, put $x = 1$, then we get

$y\left(1\right){e}^{\frac{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(1\right) - 1}{\sqrt{2}}} = 1 \implies y\left(1\right){e}^{\frac{\pi - 4}{4\sqrt{2}}} = 1 \implies y\left(1\right) = \frac{1}{{e}^{\left(\frac{\pi - 4}{4\sqrt{2}}\right)}} \implies y\left(1\right) = {e}^{\frac{4 - \pi }{4\sqrt{2}}}$

questions.question: If $y = y\left(x\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $,{e}^{y}\left(\frac{dy}{dx} - 1\right) = {e}^{x}$ such that $y\left(0\right) = 0,$ then $y\left(1\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
${e}^{y} = t {e}^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx} \frac{dt}{dx} - t = {e}^{x} IF = {e}^{ - \int dx} \implies t \cdot {e}^{ - x} = x + 1 {e}^{y - x} = x + 1 y = x + \ln ⁡\left(x + 1\right)$

at $x = 1,y = 1 + \ln ⁡\left(2\right)$

questions.question: Let $\alpha$ be a non-zero real number. Suppose $f : R \to R$ is a differentiable function such that $f\left(0\right) = 1$ and $\underset{x \to −∞}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = 1$. If ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \alpha f\left(x\right) + 3$, for all $x \in R,$ then $f\left(−{\log }_{e}2\right)$ is equal to ________.
questions.explanation:
Given: $f\left(0\right) = 1,\underset{x \to −∞}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = 1$

And ${f}^{'}\left(x\right)−\alpha \cdot f\left(x\right) = 3 \implies \frac{dy}{dx}−\alpha \cdot y = 3$

Which is a linear differential equation, so

$\implies I.F. = {e}^{−\alpha x}$

Solution of the differential equation is given by,

$y\left({e}^{−\alpha x}\right) = \int 3 \cdot {e}^{−\alpha x}dx \implies f\left(x\right)⋅\left({e}^{−\alpha x}\right) = \frac{3{e}^{−\alpha x}}{−\alpha } + c \implies f\left(x\right) = \frac{−3}{\alpha } + c \cdot {e}^{\alpha x}$

Now, taking case I: when $\alpha > 0$ and $\underset{x \to −∞}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = 1$ we get,

$\implies 1 = \frac{−3}{\alpha } + c\left(0\right) \alpha = −3$ (rejected)

Case-II: $\alpha < 0$

as $\underset{x \to −∞}{\lim }f\left(x\right) = 1 \implies c = 0 & \frac{−3}{\alpha } = 1 \left(\text{as}{e}^{ - \left( - \infty \right)} \to \infty ,\text{so }c = 0\right) \implies \alpha = −3 \implies f\left(x\right) = 1$ and also $f\left(0\right) = 1$

Hence, $f\left(x\right) = 1$ is constant function, so $f\left( - {\log }_{e}2\right) = 1$

questions.question: If $y = y\left(x\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $2{x}^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} - 2xy + 3{y}^{2} = 0$ such that $y\left(e\right) = \frac{e}{3}$, then $y\left(1\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given $2{x}^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} - 2xy + 3{y}^{2} = 0$

Dividing by $2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}$, we get,

$- \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{1}{xy} = \frac{3}{2{x}^{2}}$

Let $\frac{1}{y} = p,\frac{ - 1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dp}{dx} \implies \frac{dp}{dx} + \frac{1}{x}\left(p\right) = \frac{3}{2{x}^{2}}$

General solution will be $p \cdot {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{x}dx} = \int \frac{3}{2{x}^{2}}{ \cdot }^{{e}^{ \int \frac{1}{x}dx}}dx + c \implies \frac{x}{y} = \int \frac{3}{2x}dx + c \implies \frac{x}{y} = \frac{3}{2}\ln x + c ∵y\left(e\right) = \frac{e}{3} \implies c = \frac{3}{2} \implies \frac{x}{y} = \frac{3}{2}\ln x + \frac{3}{2}$ is the particular solution.

when $x = 1;y\left(1\right) = \frac{2}{3}$

questions.question: If $cosx\frac{dy}{dx} - ysinx = 6x$, $\left(0 < x < \frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ and $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = 0,$ then $y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
The given $D.E.$ can be written as

$\frac{dy}{dx} - y\tan x = 6x\sec x...\left(i\right),$ which is a liner differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P & Q$ are the function of $x$ or constants.

Here, $P = - \tan x & Q = 6xsecx$

Integrating factor $= {e}^{ \int Pdx} = {e}^{ - \int \tan xdx} = {e}^{ - \left( - \ln \left(\cos x\right)\right)} = {e}^{\ln \left(\cos x\right)} = \cos x$

And, the solution of the linear differential equation is,

$y\left(I.F.\right) = \int Q\left(I.F.\right)dx + c \implies y⋅\cos x = \int \left(6x\sec x\right)⋅\cos xdx \implies y⋅\cos x = \int 6xdx \implies y \cdot \cos x = 3{x}^{2} + c...\left(ii\right)$

Given $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = 0,$ hence

$0 = 3{\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)}^{2} + c \implies c = - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}$

Thus, the curve is, $y \cdot \cos x = 3{x}^{2} - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}$

Now, put $x = \frac{\pi }{6},$ to get

$y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) = 3{\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)}^{2} - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3} \implies y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)⋅\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3⋅\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{36} - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3} \implies y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)⋅\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{12} - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3} \implies y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)⋅\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} \implies y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) = - \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2\sqrt{3}}.$

questions.question: If a curve $y = f\left(x\right)$, passing through the point $\left(1,2\right)$, is the solution of the differential equation $2{x}^{2}dy = \left(2xy + {y}^{2}\right)dx$, then $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} + \frac{{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \implies {y}^{ - 2}\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}$

Put $- \frac{1}{y} = t \implies \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx} \implies \frac{dt}{dx} + \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)t = \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}$

This is a linear differential equation,

with Integrating Factor : ${e}^{ \int \frac{1}{x}dx} = {e}^{\ln \left(x\right)} = x$

So, solution of the linear differential equation is $tx = \int \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}} \cdot xdx + C \implies - \frac{x}{y} = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(x\right) + C$

The curve passes through $\left(1,2\right) \implies - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(1\right) + C \implies C = - \frac{1}{2}$

Hence, the particular solution to the differential equation is $- \frac{x}{y} = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(x\right) - \frac{1}{2} \implies \frac{x}{y} = \frac{1 - \ln \left(x\right)}{2} \implies y = \frac{2x}{1 - \ln \left(x\right)} \implies f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{2 \times \frac{1}{2}}{1 - \ln \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)} = \frac{1}{1 + \ln \left(2\right)} = \frac{1}{1 + {\log }_{e}\left(2\right)}$

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ be a solution curve of the differential equation $\left(y + 1\right){\tan }^{2}xdx + \tan xdy + ydx = 0$, $x \in \left(0,\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$. If $\underset{x \to {0}^{ + }}{\lim }xy\left(x\right) = 1$, then the value of $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)$ is:
questions.explanation:
Given:

$\left(y + 1\right){\tan }^{2}xdx + \tan xdy + ydx = 0 \implies \left(\left(y + 1\right){\tan }^{2}x + y\right)dx + \tan xdy = 0 \implies \tan x\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) + \left(y + 1\right){\tan }^{2}x + y = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + \left(1 + y\right)\tan x = - y\cot x \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + y\left(\tan x + \cot x\right) = - \tan x$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} + P\left(x\right)y = Q\left(x\right)$.

$\text{ I.F } = {e}^{ \int (\tan x + \cot x)dx} = {e}^{ \int \left(\frac{{\tan }^{2}x + 1}{\tan x}\right)dx} = {e}^{ \int \left(\frac{{\sec }^{2}x}{\tan x}\right)dx} = {e}^{{\log }_{e}\left(\tan x\right)} = \tan x\left(∵x \in \left(0,\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\right)$

Solution is

$y\tan x = \int - {\tan }^{2}xdx + c \implies y\tan x = \int \left(1 - {\sec }^{2}x\right)dx + c \implies y\tan x = x - \tan x + c$

Now,

$\underset{x \to {0}^{ + }}{\lim }xy = 1 \implies \underset{x \to {0}^{ + }}{\lim }\left(\frac{x}{\tan x}\right)\left(x - \tan x + c\right) = 1 \implies 1(0 - 0 + c) = 1 \implies c = 1$

Then the function is

$y\tan x = x - \tan x + 1$

Put $x = \frac{\pi }{4}$,

$y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\tan \left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) - \tan \left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) + 1 \implies y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{\pi }{4}$

questions.question: Let $\alpha x = \exp \left({x}^{\beta }{y}^{\gamma }\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $2{x}^{2}ydy - \left(1 - x{y}^{2}\right)dx = 0$, $x > 0,y\left(2\right) = \sqrt{{\log }_{e}2}$. Then $\alpha + \beta - \gamma$ equals :
questions.explanation:
Given the solution of differential equation,

$\alpha x = {e}^{{x}^{\beta } \cdot {y}^{\gamma }}......(1)$

Now calculating the solution of differential equation,

$2{x}^{2}y\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 - x{y}^{2}$

Let ${y}^{2} = t \implies 2\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx} ∴{x}^{2}\frac{dt}{dx} = 1 - xt \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{\mathrm{dx}} + \frac{t}{x} = \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.....(2)$

Above differential equation is linear in $t$

We know solutions of differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{\mathrm{dx}} + Py = Q$ is given by,

$y.{e}^{ \int Pdx} = \int Q.{e}^{ \int Pdx} + C({e}^{ \int Pdx} = I.F.)$

Now calculating, $I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{x}dx} = {e}^{\ln x} = x$

Therefore, the solution of equation $\left(2\right)$ is given by,

$t.x = \int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \cdot xdx + C \implies {y}^{2} \cdot x = \ln x + C ∵y(2) = \sqrt{\ln 2} ∴2.\ln 2 = \ln 2 + C \implies C = \ln 2$

Hence, solution is $x{y}^{2} = \ln x + \ln 2 \implies x{y}^{2} = \ln 2x \implies 2x = {e}^{x \cdot {y}^{2}}......(3)$

On comparing equations $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(3\right)$ we get,

$\alpha = 2,\beta = 1,\gamma = 2 ∴\alpha + \beta - \gamma = 1$

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\cos x\left(\log _{\mathrm{e}}(\cos x)\right)^2 \mathrm{dy}+\left(\sin x-3 y \sin x \log _{\mathrm{e}}(\cos x)\right) \mathrm{d} x=0, x \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$. If $y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{-1}{\log _{\mathrm{e}} 2}$, then $y\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}-\frac{3 \sin x}{\cos x \ln \cos x} y=-\frac{\sin x}{\cos x(\ln \cos x)^2} \\ & \text { I.F. }=e^{-\int \frac{3 \tan x}{\ln \cos x} d x} \\ & \text { Let } \ln \cos x=t \\ & -\tan x d x=d t \\ & e^{3 \int^{\frac{d t}{t}}}=e^{3 \ln t}=t^3=(\ln \cos x)^3 \\ & \therefore \quad \text { Solution will be } \\ & \quad y(\ln \cos x)^3=-\int(\tan x)(\ln \cos x) d x \\ & y(\ln \cos x)^3=\frac{(\ln \cos x)^2}{2}+c \\ & \because \quad y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=-\frac{1}{\ln 2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad c=0 \\ & \therefore \quad y=\frac{1}{2(\ln \cos x)} \\ & y\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{\ln \left(\cos \frac{\pi}{6}\right)} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\ln \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{\ln \sqrt{3}-\ln 2} \\ & =\frac{1}{\ln 3-\ln 4}\end{aligned}$

questions.question: Let the solution curve $y = y\left(x\right)$ of the differential equation $\left(1 + {e}^{2x}\right)\left(\frac{dy}{dx} + y\right) = 1$ pass through the point $\left(0,\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$. Then, $\underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }{e}^{x}y\left(x\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given,

$\left(1 + {e}^{2x}\right)\left(\frac{dy}{dx} + y\right) = 1$

Now on rearranging we get,

$\implies \frac{dy}{dx} + y = \frac{1}{1 + {e}^{2x}}$

We can see it is a linear differential equation,

So integrating factor is ${e}^{ \int 1 \cdot dx} = {e}^{x}$

So solution will be

$y \cdot IF = \int \frac{1}{1 + {e}^{2x}} \times IFdx \implies y{e}^{x} = \int \frac{1}{1 + {e}^{2x}} \times {e}^{x}dx \implies y \cdot {e}^{x} = {\tan }^{ - 1}\left({e}^{x}\right) + c$

Now as curve is passing through $\left(0,\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ so

$\implies c = \frac{\pi }{4}$

Now calculating the limit $\underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }\left(y \cdot {e}^{x}\right)$ we get,

$\implies \underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }\left(y \cdot {e}^{x}\right) = \underset{x \to \infty }{\lim }\left({\tan }^{ - 1}\left({e}^{x}\right) + \frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{\pi }{2} + \frac{\pi }{4} = \frac{3\pi }{4}$

questions.question: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}+2 y=\sin (2 x), y(0)=\frac{3}{4}$, then $y\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}+2 y=\sin 2 x, y(0)=\frac{3}{4} \\ & \text { I.F }=e^{\int 2 d x}=e^{2 x} \\ & y \cdot e^{2 x}=\int e^{2 x} \sin 2 x d x \\ & y \cdot e^{2 x}=\frac{e^{2 x}(2 \sin 2 x-2 \cos 2 x)}{4+4}+C \\ & x=0, y=\frac{3}{4} \Rightarrow \frac{3}{4} \cdot 1=\frac{1(0-2)}{8}+C \\ & \frac{3}{4}=-\frac{1}{4}+C \\ & 1=C \\ & y=\frac{2 \sin 2 x-2 \cos 2 x}{8}+1 \cdot e^{-2 x} \\ & x=\frac{\pi}{8}, y=\frac{1}{8}\left(2 \sin \frac{\pi}{4}-2 \cos \frac{\pi}{4}\right)+e^{-2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)} \\ & y=0+e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}}\end{aligned}$ .

questions.question: If the curve $y = y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)dy - y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)dx = 2{x}^{9 / 4}dx,x > 0$ which passes through the point $\left(1,1 - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}2\right),$ then the value of $y(16)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation is $2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)dy - y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)dx = 2{x}^{9 / 4}dx \implies 2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} - y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right) = 2{x}^{9 / 4} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)}{2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)} = \frac{2{x}^{9 / 4}}{2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)}{2x\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)} = \frac{2{x}^{9 / 4}}{2{x}^{5 / 4}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y}{2x} = \frac{x}{\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)}$

This is a linear differential equation of the type $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P = - \frac{1}{2x}$ and $Q = \frac{x}{{x}^{3 / 4} + 1}$

Now, we have integrating factor $I.F. = {e}^{ \int Pdx} = {e}^{ - \int \frac{dx}{2x}} = {e}^{ - \frac{1}{2}{\log }_{e}x} = {e}^{{\log }_{e}{x}^{ - \frac{1}{2}}} = {x}^{ - \frac{1}{2}}$

Now, the solution of the linear differential equation is $y \times \left(I.F.\right) = \int Q \times \left(I.F.\right)dx + C \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \int \frac{x \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2}}{\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)}dx + C \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \int \frac{{x}^{1 / 2}}{\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)}dx + C$

Put $x = {t}^{4} \implies dx = 4{t}^{3}dt \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \int \frac{{t}^{2} \cdot 4{t}^{3}dt}{\left({t}^{3} + 1\right)} \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = 4 \int \frac{{t}^{2}\left({t}^{3} + 1 - 1\right)}{\left({t}^{3} + 1\right)}dt \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = 4 \int {t}^{2}dt - 4 \int \frac{{t}^{2}}{{t}^{3} + 1}dt + C$

Let, ${t}^{3} + 1 = u \implies 3{t}^{2}dt = du \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = 4 \int {t}^{2}dt - \frac{4}{3} \int \frac{du}{u} + C \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \frac{4{t}^{3}}{3} - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}\left(u\right) + C \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \frac{4{t}^{3}}{3} - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}\left({t}^{3} + 1\right) + C \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \frac{4{x}^{3 / 4}}{3} - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right) + C$

Now, the curve passes through $\left(1,1 - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}2\right) \implies 1 - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}2 = \frac{4}{3} - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}2 + C \implies C = - \frac{1}{3} \implies y \cdot {x}^{ - 1 / 2} = \frac{4}{3}{x}^{3 / 4} - \frac{4}{3}{\log }_{e}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right) - \frac{1}{3} \implies y = \frac{4}{3}{x}^{5 / 4} - \frac{4}{3}\sqrt{x}{\log }_{e}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right) - \frac{\sqrt{x}}{3}$

Hence, at $x = 16,$ we get

$y(16) = \frac{4}{3} \times 32 - \frac{4}{3} \times 4 \times {\log }_{e}9 - \frac{4}{3} \implies y\left(16\right) = \frac{124}{3} - \frac{32}{3}{\log }_{e}3 \implies y\left(16\right) = 4\left(\frac{31}{3} - \frac{8}{3}{\log }_{e}3\right).$

questions.question: Let $f$ be a differentiable function such that ${x}^{2}f\left(x\right) - x = 4{ \int }_{0}^{x}tf\left(t\right)dt,f\left(1\right) = \frac{2}{3}$. Then $18f\left(3\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given,

${x}^{2}f\left(x\right) - x = 4{ \int }_{0}^{x}tf\left(t\right)dt$

Now Differentiating both side w.r.t. $x$ we get,

${x}^{2}{f}^{'}\left(x\right) + 2xf\left(x\right) - 1 = 4xf\left(x\right) \implies {x}^{2}{f}^{'}\left(x\right) - 1 = 2xf\left(x\right) \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{2}{x}y = \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \left(\mathrm{Let}y = f\left(x\right)\frac{dy}{dx} = {f}^{'}\left(x\right)\right)$

Which is a linear differential equation,

So, $I.F = {e}^{ \int - \frac{2}{x}dx} = {e}^{ - 2\ln x} = \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$

Now solution of the differential equation is given by,

$\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} = \int \frac{1}{{x}^{4}}dx + C \implies \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} = - \frac{1}{3{x}^{3}} + C$

Now given, $f\left(1\right) = \frac{2}{3}$

So, $\frac{2}{3} = - \frac{1}{3} + C \implies C = 1$

Hence, the function will be,

$f\left(x\right) = - \frac{1}{3x} + {x}^{2}$

So, the required value is given by,

$18f\left(3\right) = 18\left( - \frac{1}{9} + 9\right) = 160$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(3{x}^{2}y - y - 4{x}^{3}\right) = 0,x > 1$ with $y\left(2\right) = - 2$. Then $y\left(3\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given $x\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(3{x}^{2}y - y - 4{x}^{3}\right) = 0 \left(x - {x}^{3}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(3{x}^{2} - 1\right)y = 4{x}^{3} \frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{\left(3{x}^{2} - 1\right)}{\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)}y = \frac{4{x}^{3}}{\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$

Here $IF = {e}^{ \int Pdx} = {e}^{ \int \frac{3{x}^{2} - 1}{x - {x}^{3}}dx}$

Let $x - {x}^{3} = t \implies IF = {e}^{ \int - \frac{\mathrm{dt}}{t}} = {e}^{ - \ln t} = \frac{1}{t} ∴IF = \frac{1}{x - {x}^{3}}$

So the general solution of the differential equation will be

$y \times IF = \int Q \times IFdx y\left(\frac{1}{x - {x}^{3}}\right) = \int \frac{4{x}^{3}}{x - {x}^{3}} \times \frac{1}{\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)}dx = \int \frac{4{x}^{3}}{{\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)}^{2}}dx = \int \frac{4x}{{\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)}^{2}}dx$

Now let $I = \int \frac{4x}{{\left(1 - {x}^{2}\right)}^{2}}dx$

Substituting $1 - {x}^{2} = z I = 2 \int \frac{ - dz}{{z}^{2}} = - 2\left( - \frac{1}{z}\right) + c = \frac{2}{1 - {x}^{2}} + c$

Hence the solution of the differential equation becomes

$\frac{y}{x - {x}^{3}} = \frac{2}{1 - {x}^{2}} + c$

At $x = 2,y = - 2 \frac{ - 2}{2 - 8} = \frac{2}{1 - 4} + c \frac{1}{3} = \frac{ - 2}{3} + c ∴c = 1$

Hence the particular solution will be $\frac{y}{x - {x}^{3}} = \frac{2}{1 - {x}^{2}} + 1$

Put $x = 3 \frac{y}{3 - 27} = \frac{2}{1 - 9} + 1 \frac{y}{ - 24} = - \frac{1}{4} + 1 - \frac{y}{24} = \frac{3}{4} y = \frac{3}{4}\left( - 24\right) = - 18$

questions.explanation:

Solution will be,

Solving above with $y\left(2\right) = \frac{1 + {e}^{4}}{2{e}^{4}}$ we get,

questions.question: If $\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1 + x−{y}^{2}}{y},x\left(1\right) = 1,$ then $5x\left(2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
Given: $\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{ + } \implies \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1 + x}{y} - y \implies \frac{dx}{dy} - \frac{1 + x}{y} = - y$

Now let $1 + x = t \implies \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{dt}{dy} \implies \frac{dt}{dy} - \frac{t}{y} = - y \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ \int - \frac{1}{y}dy} \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ - \log y} \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{\log \frac{1}{y}} \implies \mathrm{IF} = \frac{1}{y}$

So, the solution of the given differential equation is

$\frac{t}{y} = \int \frac{1}{y} \times \left( - y\right)dy \implies \frac{\left(1 + x\right)}{y} = \int \frac{1}{y} \times \left( - y\right)dy \implies \frac{\left(1 + x\right)}{y} = - y + c$

Also, $x\left(1\right) = 1 \implies \frac{2}{1} = - 1 + c \implies c = 3 \implies \frac{\left(1 + x\right)}{y} = - y + 3$

Putting $y = 2 \implies \frac{\left(1 + x\right)}{2} = - 2 + 3 \implies \left(1 + x\right) = 2 \implies x = 1 \implies 5x = 5$

questions.question: Let$y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{5}{x\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)}y = \frac{{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)}^{2}}{{x}^{7}},x > 0$. If $y\left(1\right) = 2$, then $y\left(2\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given:

$\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{5}{x\left(1 + {x}^{5}\right)}y = \frac{{\left(1 + {x}^{5}\right)}^{2}}{{x}^{7}}$

This is linear differential equation.

$I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{5}{x\left(1 + {x}^{5}\right)}dx} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{5{x}^{5}}{{x}^{6}\left(1 + {x}^{5}\right)}dx} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{5}{{x}^{6}\left({x}^{ - 5} + 1\right)}dx} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - \int \frac{ - 5}{{x}^{6}\left({x}^{ - 5} + 1\right)}dx} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - \int \frac{d\left({x}^{ - 5} + 1\right)}{\left({x}^{ - 5} + 1\right)}} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - {\log }_{e}\left({x}^{ - 5} + 1\right)}\; \implies I.F. = {\left({x}^{ - 5} + 1\right)}^{ - 1} = \frac{{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)}$

So, solution is given by

$y\frac{{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)} = \int \frac{{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)} \times \frac{{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)}^{2}}{{x}^{7}}dx \implies \frac{y{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)} = \int \left(\frac{{x}^{5} + 1}{{x}^{2}}\right)dx \implies \frac{y{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)} = \int \left({x}^{3} + \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right)dx \implies \frac{y{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)} = \frac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{x} + C$

Since, $y\left(1\right) = 2$, so

$\frac{2}{2} = \frac{1}{4} - 1 + C \implies C = \frac{7}{4}$

So,

$\frac{y{x}^{5}}{\left({x}^{5} + 1\right)} = \frac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{x} + \frac{7}{4}$

Put $x = 2$, then we get

$\frac{y\left(2\right) \times 32}{33} = \frac{16}{4} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{7}{4} \implies y\left(2\right) = \frac{21 \times 33}{128} = \frac{693}{128}$

questions.question:
If $y = y\left(x\right),x \in \left(0,\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation

$\left({\sin }^{2}2x\right)\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(8{\sin }^{2}2x + 2\sin 4x\right)y = 2{e}^{ - 4x}\left(2\sin 2x + \cos 2x\right),$ with $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = {e}^{ - \pi }$, then $y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given, $\left({\sin }^{2}2x\right)\frac{dy}{dx} + \left(8{\sin }^{2}2x + 2\sin 4x\right)y = 2{e}^{ - 4x}\left(2\sin 2x + \cos 2x\right)$

Now rewriting the given differential equation we get,

$\implies \frac{dy}{dx} + \left(8 + 4\cot 2x\right)y = \frac{2{e}^{ - 4x}}{{\sin }^{2}2x}\left(2\sin x + \cos 2x\right)$

Which is a linear differential equation.

Now calculating $IF = {e}^{ \int \left(8 + 4\cot 2x\right)\mathrm{dx}} = {e}^{8x + 2\ln \left(\sin 2x\right)} = {e}^{8x} \cdot {\sin }^{2}2x$

Now solution of differential equation is given by,

$y \times IF = \int \frac{2{e}^{ - 4x}\left(2\sin 2x + \cos 2x\right)}{{\sin }^{2}2x} \times IFdx \implies y\left({e}^{8x} \cdot {\sin }^{2}2x\right) = \int 2{e}^{4x}\left(2\sin 2x + \cos 2x\right)dx \implies y\left({e}^{8x} \cdot {\sin }^{2}2x\right) = {e}^{4x} \cdot \sin 2x + C$

Now given $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = {e}^{ - \pi } \implies C = 0$

So, the equation of curve is given by $y = \frac{{e}^{ - 4x}}{\sin 2x}$

So, the value of $y\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) = \frac{{e}^{ - 4\frac{\pi }{6}}}{\sin \left(2 \cdot \frac{\pi }{6}\right)} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}{e}^{ - \frac{2\pi }{3}}$

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left(1+x^2\right) \frac{d y}{d x}+y=e^{\tan ^{-1} x}$, $y(1)=0$. Then $y(0)$ is
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{y}{1+x^2}=\frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} x}}{1+x^2} \\ & \text { I.F. }=e^{\int \frac{1}{1+x^2} d x}=e^{\tan ^{-1} x} \\ & y \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} x}=\int\left(\frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} x}}{1+x^2}\right) e^{\tan ^{-1} x} \cdot d x \\ & \text { Let } \tan ^{-1} x=z \quad \therefore \frac{d x}{1+x^2}=d z \\ & \therefore y \cdot e^z=\int e^{2 z} d z=\frac{e^{2 z}}{2}+C \\ & y \cdot e^{\tan ^{-1} x}=\frac{e^{2 \tan ^{-1} x}}{2}+C \\ & \Rightarrow y=\frac{e^{\tan ^{-1} x}}{2}+\frac{C}{e^{\tan ^{-1} x}}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \because \mathrm{y}(1)=0 \Rightarrow 0=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 4}}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 4}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{C}=\frac{-\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}}{2} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{y}=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{x}}}{2}-\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}}{2 \mathrm{e}^{\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{x}}} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{y}(0)=\frac{1-\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}}{2}\end{aligned}$

Integrating factor, $I.F. = {e}^{ \int \frac{3\text{ }dx}{4x}} = {e}^{\frac{3}{4}lnx} = {x}^{\frac{3}{4}}$

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ satisfies the equation $\frac{dy}{dx} - \left(A\right) = 0,$ for all $x > 0,$ where $A = \left( \begin{matrix}y & \sin x & 1 \\ 0 & - 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & \frac{1}{x}\end{matrix} \right)$. If $y(\pi ) = \pi + 2,$ then the value of $y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ is:
questions.explanation:
We have,

$A = \left( \begin{matrix}y & \sin x & 1 \\ 0 & - 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & \frac{1}{x}\end{matrix} \right) \implies \left(A\right) = - \frac{y}{x} + 2\sin x + 2$

Now,

$\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(A\right) \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = - \frac{y}{x} + 2\sin x + 2 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{y}{x} = 2\sin x + 2 \text{I.F.} = {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{x}dx} = x$

Solution is

$y \times \left(I.F.\right) = \int \left(I.F.\right) \times \left(2\sin x + 2\right)dx \implies yx = \int x(2\sin x + 2)dx \implies yx = 2 \int x\left(\sin x\right)dx + 2 \int xdx \implies xy = {x}^{2} - 2x\cos x + 2\sin x + c \dots \left(i\right)$

Now $x = \pi ,y = \pi + 2$, hence

$\implies \pi \left(\pi + 2\right) = {\pi }^{2} - 2\pi \left( - 1\right) + 0 + c \implies c = 0$

Now $\left(i\right)$ becomes

$xy = {x}^{2} - 2x\cos x + 2\sin x$

Put $x = \frac{\pi }{2}$, then

$\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)y = {\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}^{2} - 2 \cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cos \left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) + 2\sin \left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \implies \left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)y = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} + 2 \implies y = \frac{\pi }{2} + \frac{4}{\pi }$

questions.question: If $\frac{dy}{dx} + {e}^{x}\left({x}^{2}−2\right)y = \left({x}^{2}−2x\right)\left({x}^{2}−2\right){e}^{2x}$ and $y\left(0\right) = 0$, then the value of $y\left(2\right)$ is
questions.explanation:
Given

$\frac{dy}{dx} + {e}^{x}\left({x}^{2}−2\right)y = \left({x}^{2}−2x\right)\left({x}^{2}−2\right){e}^{2x}$

It is linear differential equation so,

$IF = {e}^{ \int \left({x}^{2} - 2\right){e}^{x}dx} = {e}^{{x}^{2}{e}^{x} - 2 \int x{e}^{x}dx - 2{e}^{x}} = {e}^{{x}^{2}{e}^{x} - 2\left(x{e}^{x} - {e}^{x}\right) - 2{e}^{x}} IF = {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}}$

Now solution is given by

$y \times {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} = \int {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} \times \left({x}^{2} - 2x\right)\left({x}^{2} - 2\right){e}^{2x} = \int {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} \times \left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}\left({x}^{2} - 2\right){e}^{x}$

Now let $\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x} = t$

We get ${e}^{x}\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right) + {e}^{x}\left(2x - 2\right)dx = dt {e}^{x}\left({x}^{2} - 2x + 2x - 2\right)dx = dt {e}^{x}\left({x}^{2} - 2\right)dx = dt y \times {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} = \int {e}^{t} \times t \times dt y \times {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} = {e}^{t}\left(t - 1\right) + c y \times {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} = {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}}\left(\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x} - 1\right) + c$

Now at $x = 0y = 0 0 \times {e}^{0} = {e}^{0}\left(0x{e}^{x} - 1\right) + c 0 = - 1 + c c = 1$

Putting the value of $c = 1$ we get the equation as

$\implies y \times {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}} = {e}^{\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x}}\left(\left({x}^{2} - 2x\right){e}^{x} - 1\right) + 1$

Now putting $x = 2$ in equation we get

$y \times {e}^{\left(4 - 4\right){e}^{2}} = {e}^{\left(4 - 4\right){e}^{2}}\left(\left(4 - 4\right){e}^{2} - 1\right) + 1 \implies y \times {e}^{0} = {e}^{0}\left(\left(0\right){e}^{2} - 1\right) + 1 \implies y = - 1 + 1 = 0$

questions.question: Let $y = {y}_{1}\left(x\right)$ and $y = {y}_{2}\left(x\right)$ be two distinct solutions of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$, with ${y}_{1}\left(0\right) = 0$ and ${y}_{2}\left(0\right) = 1$ respectively. Then, the number of points of intersection of $y = {y}_{1}\left(x\right)$ and $y = {y}_{2}\left(x\right)$ is

Given,

$\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - y = x$

So, $IF = {e}^{ \int - 1dx} = {e}^{ - x}$

Now solution is given by $y{e}^{ - x} = \int x{e}^{ - x}dx \implies y{e}^{ - x} = - x{e}^{ - x} - {e}^{ - x} + c \implies y = - x - 1 + c{e}^{x}$

Also given ${y}_{2}\left(0\right) = 1 \implies c = 2 ∴{y}_{2} = - x - 1 + 2{e}^{x}⋯\left(2\right)$

Now from equation $\left(1\right) & \left(2\right)$ we get, ${y}_{2} - {y}_{1} = {e}^{x} > 0∴{y}_{2} \ne {y}_{1} ∴$ Number of points of intersection of ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ is zero.

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\left(\tan x\right) + y}{\sin x\left(\sec x - \sin x\tan x\right)},x \in \left(0,\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ satisfying the condition $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = 2$. Then, $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)$ is
questions.explanation:
Given: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\tan x + y}{\sin x\left(\sec x - \sin x\tan x\right)} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\tan x + y}{\sin x\left(\frac{1}{\cos x} - \frac{{\sin }^{2}x}{\cos x}\right)} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\tan x + y}{\sin x\left(\frac{{\cos }^{2}x}{\cos x}\right)} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\tan x + y}{\sin x\cos x} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{2y}{\sin 2x} = {\sec }^{2}x \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ - 2 \int \mathrm{cosec}2xdx} \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ - \log \left(\mathrm{cosec}2x - \cot 2x\right)} \implies \mathrm{IF} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{cosec}2x - \cot 2x} = \mathrm{cosec}2x + \cot 2x \implies \mathrm{IF} = \frac{1}{\sin 2x} + \frac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} \implies \mathrm{IF} = \frac{2{\cos }^{2}x}{2\sin x\cos x} \implies \mathrm{IF} = \cot x \implies y \times \cot x = \int \cot x \times {\sec }^{2}xdx \implies y \times \cot x = 2 \int \mathrm{cosec}2xdx \implies y\cot x = \log \left(\mathrm{cosec}2x - \cot 2x\right) + c$

Now, using $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = 2$ we get,

$\implies 2\cot \frac{\pi }{4} = \log \left(\mathrm{cosec}\frac{\pi }{2} - \cot \frac{\pi }{2}\right) + c \implies c = 2 \implies y\cot x = \log \left(\mathrm{cosec}2x - \cot 2x\right) + 2$

Now, finding $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)$ we get,

$\implies y\cot \frac{\pi }{3} = \log \left(\mathrm{cosec}\frac{2\pi }{3} - \cot \frac{2\pi }{3}\right) + 2 \implies y \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \log \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + 2 \implies y \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{2}\log 3 + 2 \implies y = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\log 3 + 2\sqrt{3} \implies y = \sqrt{3}\left(\log \sqrt{3} + 2\right)$

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation ${x}^{3}dy + (xy–1)dx = 0,x > 0, y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 3 - e$. Then $y\left(1\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation is

${x}^{3}dy + \left(xy - 1\right)dx = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 - xy}{{x}^{3}} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{{x}^{3}} - \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} = \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}$

This is a linear differential equation.

If $\mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ \int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}dx} = {e}^{ - \frac{1}{x}}$

Solution of a given linear differential equation is

$y{e}^{ - \frac{1}{x}} = \int {e}^{ - \frac{1}{x}}\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\right)dx$

Put $- \frac{1}{x} = t \implies \frac{dx}{{x}^{2}} = dt \implies y{e}^{ - \frac{1}{x}} = - \int {e}^{ - t}tdt \implies y{e}^{ - \frac{1}{x}} = t{e}^{ - t} + {e}^{ - t} + C \implies y = t + 1 + C{e}^{\frac{1}{x}} \implies y = \frac{1}{x} + 1 + C{e}^{\frac{1}{x}}$

Put $x = \frac{1}{2}$, then

$3 - e = 2 + 1 + C{e}^{2} C = - \frac{1}{e}$

So,

$y = \frac{1}{x} + 1 - \frac{1}{e}\left({e}^{\frac{1}{x}}\right)$

So,

$y\left(1\right) = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation ${cosec}^{2}xdy + 2dx = \left(1 + y\cos 2x\right){cosec}^{2}xdx,$ with $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = 0.$ Then, the value of ${\left(y\left(0\right) + 1\right)}^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
Given, ${cosec}^{2}xdy + 2dx = \left(1 + y\cos 2x\right){cosec}^{2}xdx \implies \frac{dy}{{\sin }^{2}x} + 2dx = \left(\frac{1 + y\cos 2x}{{\sin }^{2}x}\right)dx \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + 2{\sin }^{2}x = 1 + y\cos 2x \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + 2{\sin }^{2}x - 1 = y\cos 2x$

Using, $\cos 2x = 1 - 2{\sin }^{2}x,$ we get

$\frac{dy}{dx} + \left( - \cos 2x\right) = y\cos 2x \implies \frac{dy}{dx} + \left( - \cos 2x\right)y = \cos 2x$

This is a linear differential equation of the type $\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P & Q$ are the functions of $x$ or constants.

Thus, $P = - \cos 2x & Q = \cos 2x$

Now, we have integrating factor I.F.$= {e}^{ \int Pdx} = {e}^{ \int - cos2xdx} = {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)}$

And, the solution of the given differential equation is

$y\left(I.F.\right) = \int Q\left(I.F.\right)dx + c \implies y \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} = \int \left(\cos 2x\right) \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)}dx + c$

Put $\frac{\sin 2x}{2} = t, \implies \frac{2\cos 2x}{2}dx = dt \implies y \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} = \int {e}^{ - t}dt + c \implies y \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} = - {e}^{ - t}dt + c \implies y \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} = - {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} + c$

Given, $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = 0 \implies 0 \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin \left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{2}\right)} = - {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin \left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{2}\right)} + c \implies c = - {e}^{ - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)} \implies y \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} = - {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)} + {e}^{ - \frac{1}{2}}$

Now, at $x = 0 \implies y\left(0\right) \cdot {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 0}{2}\right)} = - {e}^{ - \left(\frac{\sin 0}{2}\right)} + {e}^{ - \frac{1}{2}} \implies y\left(0\right) \cdot {e}^{0} = - {e}^{0} + {e}^{ - \frac{1}{2}} \implies y\left(0\right) = - 1 + {e}^{ - \frac{1}{2}} \implies y\left(0\right) + 1 = {e}^{ - \frac{1}{2}} \implies {\left(y\left(0\right) + 1\right)}^{2} = {e}^{ - 1}.$

questions.question: If $\frac{dy}{dx} + 2y\tan x = \sin x,0 < x < \frac{\pi }{2}$ and $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = 0$, then the maximum value of $y\left(x\right)$ is
questions.explanation:
We know that,

$\frac{dy}{dx} + y\left(2\tan x\right) = \sin x$ is a linear differential equation so,

$I.F = {e}^{ \int 2\tan xdx} = {e}^{2\ln \left(\sec x\right)} = {\sec }^{2}x$

The general solution will be

$y{\sec }^{2}x = \int \sin x{\sec }^{2}xdx + C \implies y{\sec }^{2}x = \sec x + C ∵y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = 0 \implies C = - 2$

Hence the particular solution is

$y{\sec }^{2}x = \sec x - 2 \implies y = \cos x - 2{\cos }^{2}x \implies y = \frac{1}{8} - 2{\left(\cos x - \frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}$

So, the maximum value of $y\left(x\right)$ is $\frac{1}{8}$

questions.question: If a curve passes through the origin and the slope of the tangent to it at any point $\left(x,y\right)$ is $\frac{{x}^{2} - 4x + y + 8}{x - 2},$ then this curve also passes through the point:
questions.explanation:
Given

$y\left(0\right) = 0$

and $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{{\left(x - 2\right)}^{2} + y + 4}{x - 2} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y}{x - 2} = \left(x - 2\right) + \frac{4}{x - 2} \implies I.F. = {e}^{ - \int \frac{1}{x - 2}dx} = \frac{1}{x - 2}$

Solution of L.D.E.

$\implies y\frac{1}{x - 2} = \int \frac{1}{x - 2}\left(\left(x - 2\right) + \frac{4}{x - 2}\right) \cdot dx \implies \frac{y}{x - 2} = x - \frac{4}{x - 2} + C$

Now, at $x = 0,y = 0 \implies C = - 2 y = x\left(x - 2\right) - 4 - 2\left(x - 2\right) \implies y = {x}^{2} - 4x$

This curve passes through $\left(5,5\right)$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{\sqrt{2}y}{2{\cos }^{4}x - \cos 2x} = x{e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)},0 < x < \frac{\pi }{2}$ with $y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{32}$. If $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{18}{e}^{ - {\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\alpha \right)}$, then the value of $3{\alpha }^{2}$ is equal to ______.
questions.explanation:
Given $\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2{\cos }^{4}x - \cos 2x}y = x{e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)}$

This is a linear differential equation.

Here $I = \int \frac{dx}{2{\cos }^{4}x - \cos 2x} = \int \frac{dx}{\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{{\cos }^{2}2x}{2} + \cos 2x\right) - \cos 2x} = 2\sqrt{2} \int \frac{{\sec }^{2}2xdx}{2 + {\tan }^{2}2x}$

Put $\tan 2x = t I = {\tan }^{ - 1}\frac{\tan 2x}{\sqrt{2}} ∴IF = {e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\frac{\tan 2x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)} = {e}^{{\cot }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)}$

So general solution will be

$y{e}^{{\cot }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)} = \int x{e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)}{e}^{{\cot }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)}dx y{e}^{{\cot }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)} = {e}^{\frac{\pi }{2}}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) + c y\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{32} \implies c = 0$

i.e. $y = \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot 2x\right)}$

Given $y\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{18}{e}^{ - {\tan }^{ - 1}\alpha } \implies \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{18}{e}^{ - {\tan }^{ - 1}\alpha } = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{18}{e}^{{\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{2}\cot \frac{2\pi }{3}\right)} = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{18}{e}^{ - {\tan }^{ - 1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right)}$

Hence $\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \implies 3{\alpha }^{2} = 2$

questions.question: For a differentiable function $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, suppose $f^{\prime}(x)=3 f(x)+\alpha$, where $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(0)=1$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=7$. Then $9 f\left(-\log _{\mathrm{e}} 3\right)$ is equal to_________
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}-3 y=\alpha \\ & \text { If }=e^{\int-3 d x}=e^{-3 x} \\ & \therefore \quad y-e^{-3 x}=\int e^{-3 x} \cdot \alpha d x \\ & y e^{-3 x}=\frac{\alpha e^{-3 x}}{-3}+c \\ & \left(* e^{3 x}\right) \\ & y=\frac{\alpha}{-3}+C \cdot e^{3 x}\end{aligned}$ on substituting $\mathrm{x}=0, \mathrm{y}=1 x \rightarrow-\infty, y=7$ we get $y=7-6 e^{3 x} 9 f\left(-\log _e 3\right)=61$

questions.question:
Let $y = y(x)$ be solution of the following differential equation

${e}^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} - 2{e}^{y}\sin x + \sin x{\cos }^{2}x = 0,y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) = 0$.

If $y\left(0\right) = {\log }_{e}\left(\alpha + \beta {e}^{ - 2}\right)$, then $4(\alpha + \beta )$ is equal to <u> </u>.
questions.explanation:
Let ${e}^{y} = t \implies {e}^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx}$

So,

${e}^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} - 2{e}^{y}\sin x + \sin x{\cos }^{2}x = 0 \implies \frac{dt}{dx} - \left(2\sin x\right)t = - \sin x{\cos }^{2}x$

So, the integrating factor $I.F. = {e}^{ \int - 2\sin xdx} = {e}^{2\cos x}$

So, the solution of differential equation is

$t \cdot {e}^{2\cos x} = \int {e}^{2\cos x} \cdot \left( - \sin x{\cos }^{2}x\right)dx \implies {e}^{y} \cdot {e}^{2\cos x} = \int {e}^{2z} \cdot {z}^{2}dz$ (Assume, $z = \cos x \implies dz = - \sin x$)

Using integration by parts,

$\implies {e}^{y} \cdot {e}^{2\cos x} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot {z}^{2} \cdot {e}^{2z} - \frac{1}{2}z \cdot {e}^{2z} + \frac{{e}^{2z}}{4} + C \implies {e}^{y} \cdot {e}^{2\cos x} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot {\cos }^{2}x \cdot {e}^{2\cos x} - \frac{1}{2}\cos x \cdot {e}^{2\cos x} + \frac{{e}^{2\cos x}}{4} + C$

at $x = \frac{\pi }{2},y = 0 \implies C = \frac{3}{4} \implies {e}^{y} = \frac{1}{2}{\cos }^{2}x - \frac{1}{2}\cos x + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} \cdot {e}^{ - 2\cos x}$

Put $x = 0 \implies y = \log \left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4}{e}^{ - 2}\right) \implies \alpha = \frac{1}{4},\beta = \frac{3}{4}$

So, $\alpha + \beta = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} = 1$

questions.question: Let $f$ be a differentiable function such that $2(x+2)^2 f(x)-3(x+2)^2=10 \int_0^x(t+2) f(t) d t, x \geq 0$. Then $f(2)$ is equal to ______.
questions.explanation:
$2(x+2)^2 f(x)-3(x+2)^2=10 \int_0^x(t+2) f(t) d t$
Differentiating both side
$\begin{aligned}
& 4(x+2) f(x)+2 f(x)(x+2)^2-6(x+2)=10(x+2) f(x) \\
& =(x+2) $\frac{d y}{d x}$-3 y=3 \\
& $\frac{1}{3} \int \frac{d y}{y+1} = \int \frac{d x}{x+2}$ \\
& $\ln$ |y+1=3 $\ln$ | x+2 $\mid + \ln$ c \\
& y+1=(x+2)^3 c \\
& $\because$ y(0)=$\frac{3}{2}$ \\
& $\Rightarrow \frac{5}{16}$=c \\
& $\therefore \quad$ y=$\frac{5}{16}$(x+2)^3-1 \\
& y(2)=$\frac{5}{16}$ \times 64-1=19
\end{aligned}$

questions.question: If $x = x\left(t\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $\left(t + 1\right)dx = \left(2x + {\left(t + 1\right)}^{4}\right)dt,x\left(0\right) = 2$, then $x\left(1\right)$ equals ________
questions.explanation:
Given: $\left(t + 1\right)dx = \left(2x + {\left(t + 1\right)}^{4}\right)dt \implies \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{2x + {\left(t + 1\right)}^{4}}{\left(t + 1\right)} \implies \frac{dx}{dt} - \frac{2x}{\left(t + 1\right)} = {\left(t + 1\right)}^{3} \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ \int \frac{ - 2}{t + 1}dt} \implies \mathrm{IF} = {e}^{ - 2\log \left(t + 1\right)} \implies \mathrm{IF} = \frac{1}{{\left(t + 1\right)}^{2}}$

Solution of the differential equations is given by,

$\implies x \times \frac{1}{{\left(t + 1\right)}^{2}} = \int \left(t + 1\right)dt \implies \frac{x}{{\left(t + 1\right)}^{2}} = \frac{{t}^{2}}{2} + t + c$

It is given that $x\left(0\right) = 2 \implies \frac{2}{{\left(0 + 1\right)}^{2}} = \frac{0}{2} + 0 + c \implies c = 2 \implies \frac{x}{{\left(t + 1\right)}^{2}} = \frac{{t}^{2}}{2} + t + 2$

Putting $t = 1$,

$\implies \frac{x}{{\left(1 + 1\right)}^{2}} = \frac{{1}^{2}}{2} + 1 + 2 \implies \frac{x}{4} = \frac{1}{2} + 3 \implies x = 2 + 12 \implies x = 14$

questions.question: The slope of normal at any point $\left(x,y\right),x > 0,y > 0$ on the curve $y = y\left(x\right)$ is given by $\frac{{x}^{2}}{xy - {x}^{2}{y}^{2} - 1}$. If the curve passes through the point $\left(1,1\right)$, then $e \cdot y\left(e\right)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
Given,

Slope of normal $= \frac{ - dx}{dy} = \frac{{x}^{2}}{xy - {x}^{2}{y}^{2} - 1} {x}^{2}{y}^{2}dx + dx - xydx = {x}^{2}dy {x}^{2}{y}^{2}dx + dx = {x}^{2}dy + xydx {x}^{2}{y}^{2}dx + dx = x\left(xdy + ydx\right) {x}^{2}{y}^{2}dx + dx = xd\left(xy\right) \frac{dx}{x} = \frac{dxy}{1 + {x}^{2}{y}^{2}} \ln kx = {\tan }^{ - 1}\left(xy\right)⋯\left(i\right)$

Curve passes though $\left(1,1\right)$

So, In $k = \frac{\pi }{4} \implies k = {e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}$

Now from equation $\left(i\right)$

We get, $\frac{\pi }{4} + \ln x = {\tan }^{ - 1}\left(xy\right) xy = \tan \left(\frac{\pi }{4} + ℓnx\right) xy = \left(\frac{1 + \tan \left(ℓnx\right)}{1 - \tan \left(ℓnx\right)}\right)⋯\left(\mathrm{ii}\right)$

Put $x = e$ in $\left(\mathrm{ii}\right)$

We get,$e.y\left(e\right) = \frac{1 + \tan 1}{1 - \tan 1}$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)dy = \left(y + y{x}^{2} - 3{x}^{4}\right)dx,x > 2$ If $y\left(3\right) = 3,$ then $y\left(4\right)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
$\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)dy = \left(y + y{x}^{2} - 3{x}^{4}\right)dx \implies xdy - ydx = \left(y{x}^{2} - 3{x}^{4}\right)dx + {x}^{3}dy \implies \frac{xdy - ydx}{{x}^{2}} = (ydx + xdy) - 3{x}^{2}dx \implies d\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = d\left(xy\right) - d\left({x}^{3}\right)$

Integrate

$\implies \frac{y}{x} = xy - {x}^{3} + c$

given $f\left(3\right) = 3 \implies \frac{3}{3} = 3 \times 3 - {3}^{3} + c \implies c = 19 ∴\frac{y}{x} = xy - {x}^{3} + 19$

at $x = 4,\frac{y}{4} = 4y - 64 + 19 15y = 4 \times 45 \implies y = 12$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $xdy = \left(y + {x}^{3}\cos x\right)dx$ with $y\left(\pi \right) = 0,$ then $y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
We have, $xdy = \left(y + {x}^{3}\cos x\right)dx \implies xdy = ydx + {x}^{3}\cos xdx \implies \frac{xdy - ydx}{{x}^{2}} = \frac{{x}^{3}\cos xdx}{{x}^{2}} \implies \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \int x\cos xdx \implies \frac{y}{x} = x\sin x - \int 1.\sin xdx$

Therefore, $\frac{y}{x} = x\sin x + \cos x + C$

At $x = \pi ,y = 0, 0 = - 1 + C \implies C = 1,x = \pi ,y = 0$

So, $\frac{y}{x} = x\sin x + \cos x + 1 \implies y = {x}^{2}\sin x + x\cos x + x$

Hence, $y\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) = \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} + \frac{\pi }{2}.$
